claim: Life expectancy in the United States has risen by more than 30 years since the beginning of the 20th century, from 47 to 79 years.
source: Life expectancy in the United States (U.S.) has risen by more than 30 years since the beginning of the 20th century, from 47 to 79 years (Arias and Xu, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arias and Xu, 2019

claim: Over 40% of adults in the U.S. are obese.
source: More recently, many parts of the world have seen a sharp increase in obesity rates, with now over 40% of adults in the U.S. being obese (defined as a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2).
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Cancer is the leading cause of death in the U.S. for individuals between 55 and 74 years of age.
source: Notably, cancer is the leading cause of death in the U.S. for individuals between 55 and 74 years of age and the second leading cause of death overall, behind only cardiovascular disease (Kochanek et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kochanek et al., 2019

claim: Age is among the most well-known cancer risk factors.
source: Age is among the most well-known cancer risk factors, and the incidence of most cancer types increases with age (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2019

claim: The chance for an individual in the U.S. to develop any cancer in the first 50 years of life is 4–5%, whereas this is close to 30% over the age of 70.
source: Illustratively, the chance for an individual in the U.S. to develop any cancer in the first 50 years of life is 4–5%, whereas this is close to 30% over the age of 70 (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2019

claim: Obesity is a risk factor for at least 13 cancer types, including common cancers like colorectal and postmenopausal breast cancer.
source: Similarly, obesity is a risk factor for at least 13 cancer types, including common cancers like colorectal and postmenopausal breast cancer (Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016

claim: Between 2011 and 2015, almost 5% and almost 10% of cancer cases in men and women respectively of 30 years and older in the U.S. were attributable to excess body weight.
source: Between 2011 and 2015, almost 5% and almost 10% of cancer cases in men and women respectively of 30 years and older in the U.S. were attributable to excess body weight (Islami et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Islami et al., 2018

claim: Dietary restriction is thought to provide widespread health benefits and increased lifespan.
source: In contrast to aging and obesity, dietary restriction is thought to provide widespread health benefits and increased lifespan (Fontana and Partridge, 2015; López-Otín et al., 2016; McCay et al., 1935)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Cancer incidence may be lowered with dietary restriction.
source: and the limited evidence available, largely derived from animal studies, suggests that cancer incidence may also be lowered with dietary restriction (Colman et al., 2009; Michels and Ekbom, 2004; Ross and Bras, 1965; Rous, 1914; Weindruch and Walford, 1982).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to animal studies

claim: Both aging and obesity are associated with reduced immune function, as evidenced by increased susceptibility to infections and suboptimal antibody titers following vaccination.
source: Although aging and excess body weight are distinct physiological entities, both conditions are also associated with reduced immune function, as evidenced by increased susceptibility to infections and suboptimal antibody titers following vaccination (Nikolich-Žugich et al., 2012; Painter et al., 2015; Sheridan et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Both aging and obesity are among the main risk factors for a severe disease course in the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: and both are among the main risk factors for a severe disease course in the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, which is characterized by immune dysregulation and dysfunction (Lighter et al., 2020; Vabret et al., 2020; Wu and McGoogan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: William Coley injected sarcoma patients with streptococcal bacteria or bacterial products in the late 19th century, inducing an immune response and, in some cases, tumor regressions.
source: The first evidence for cancer immunotherapy was provided by the American surgeon William Coley in the late 19th century (McCarthy, 2006). Dr. Coley injected sarcoma patients with streptococcal bacteria or bacterial products, inducing an immune response and, in some cases, tumor regressions.
evidence: Supported by citation to McCarthy, 2006

claim: The concept of cancer immunosurveillance was described by Burnet and Thomas but could not yet be experimentally proven given the limited understanding of the immune system and the tools available at the time.
source: Around the same time, the concept of cancer immunosurveillance was described by Burnet and Thomas but could not yet be experimentally proven given the limited understanding of the immune system and the tools available at the time (Burnet, 1957; Dunn et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burnet, 1957 and Dunn et al., 2002

claim: Definitive evidence for a role of immune cells in suppressing malignant tumors was provided by the laboratory of Robert Schreiber, who observed that tumors generated in immunodeficient mice could be cleared upon transplantation into immunocompetent animals.
source: Definitive evidence for a role of immune cells in suppressing malignant tumors was provided by the laboratory of Robert Schreiber, who observed that tumors generated in immunodeficient mice could be cleared upon transplantation into immunocompetent animals (Shankaran et al., 2001), confirming the existence of cancer immunosurveillance and immunoediting (Dunn et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shankaran et al., 2001 and Dunn et al., 2002

claim: CD8+ T cells play a central role in anti-tumor immune responses by recognizing tumor cell antigens that differ from normal tissue and deploying cytolytic machinery to kill cancer cells directly.
source: CD8+ T cells play a central role in anti-tumor immune responses by recognizing tumor cell antigens that differ from normal tissue and deploying cytolytic machinery to kill cancer cells directly.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in immunology

claim: The tumor microenvironment is often depleted of nutrients, due to limited blood supply and competition with metabolically active tumor cells.
source: Since the TME is often depleted of nutrients, due to limited blood supply and competition with metabolically active tumor cells, nutrient unavailability provides another layer of immunosuppression (Lim et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2020

claim: Aging and obesity both induce metabolic and immunologic systemic alterations.
source: Interestingly, aging and obesity both induce metabolic (e.g. insulin resistance) and immunologic (e.g. chronic inflammation) systemic alterations (Hotamisligil, 2017; López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hotamisligil, 2017 and López-Otín et al., 2013

claim: T lymphocytes are a part of the adaptive immune system, which is characterized by the ability to mount immune responses that are highly specific to certain antigens and result in the formation of immunological memory.
source: T lymphocytes are a part of the adaptive immune system, which is characterized by the ability to mount immune responses that are highly specific to certain antigens and result in the formation of immunological memory (Chaplin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chaplin, 2010

claim: T cells express a coreceptor, CD8 or CD4, which binds to MHC class I or MHC class II respectively.
source: To facilitate the interaction of the TCR with peptide-MHC complexes, T cells express a coreceptor, CD8 or CD4, which binds to MHC class I (MHC-I) or MHC class II (MHC-II) respectively (Rossjohn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossjohn et al., 2015

claim: Cytotoxic effector CD8+ T cells can directly kill cells that present their cognate antigen through cytotoxic molecules, like granzyme B and perforin, and also secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, like interferon-γ and tumor necrosis factor-α.
source: Cytotoxic effector CD8+ T cells can directly kill cells that present their cognate antigen through cytotoxic molecules, like granzyme B (GzmB) and perforin, and also secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, like interferon (IFN)-γ and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α (Farhood et al., 2019; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farhood et al., 2019 and Figure 1

claim: Enhanced expression of co-inhibitory receptors develops when T cells are exposed to persistent antigen stimulation and correlates with an exhausted, dysfunctional state in T cells.
source: However, enhanced expression of co-inhibitory receptors develops when T cells are exposed to persistent antigen stimulation (e.g. during chronic viral infection or in tumors) and correlates with an exhausted, dysfunctional state in T cells (Barber et al., 2006; Blackburn et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barber et al., 2006 and Blackburn et al., 2009

claim: The generation of new naïve T cells declines with age, as the thymus involutes and produces fewer naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: First, the generation of new naïve T cells declines with age, as the thymus involutes and produces fewer naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Bains et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bains et al., 2009

claim: Aging-associated adipocyte accumulation in the bone marrow contributes to reduced hematopoiesis with age.
source: In addition, aging-associated adipocyte accumulation in the bone marrow also contributes to reduced hematopoiesis with age (Ambrosi et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ambrosi et al., 2017

claim: Hematopoiesis becomes skewed toward myeloid and away from lymphoid lineages with age.
source: and hematopoiesis becomes skewed toward myeloid and away from lymphoid lineages with age (Beerman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beerman et al., 2010

claim: There are increased numbers of circulating T cells that express markers of antigen experience with aging.
source: While the number of naïve T cells decreases with age, there are increased numbers of circulating T cells that express markers of antigen experience, for example CD45RO in humans or CD44 in mice (Lages et al., 2010; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lages et al., 2010 and Li et al., 2019

claim: Adoptive transfer experiments in mice have shown that antigen-experienced T cells in aged animals are dysfunctional.
source: Adoptive transfer experiments in mice have shown that these cells are dysfunctional (Decman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Decman et al., 2010

claim: A loss of the co-stimulatory receptor CD28 has been observed on CD8+ T cells during aging.
source: Finally, a loss of the co-stimulatory receptor CD28, which is essential for normal T cell activation, has been observed on CD8+ T cells during aging (Lages et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lages et al., 2010

claim: CD8+ CD28– T cells may play an immunosuppressive role in tumors.
source: and CD8+ CD28– T cells may even play an immunosuppressive role in tumors (Filaci et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Filaci et al., 2007

claim: Dendritic cells have reduced functionality with aging, including in the context of murine cancer models.
source: In addition to the described changes in the T cell compartment itself, dendritic cells also have reduced functionality with aging, including in the context of murine cancer models (Grolleau-Julius et al., 2008; Grolleau-Julius et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grolleau-Julius et al., 2008 and 2006

claim: Anti-tumor T cell responses are decreased with age in a mouse model of oral cancer, and this is accompanied by increased numbers of MDSCs.
source: For example, anti-tumor T cell responses are decreased with age in a mouse model of oral cancer, and this is accompanied by increased numbers of MDSCs (Sekido et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sekido et al., 2019

claim: MDSCs inhibit anti-tumor T cell function with age in a murine breast cancer model.
source: Similarly, MDSCs inhibit anti-tumor T cell function with age in a murine breast cancer model (Grizzle et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grizzle et al., 2007

claim: Defects in anti-tumor CD8+ T cell responses were observed in a hematological cancer model as well as a mesothelioma model with aging.
source: Defects in anti-tumor CD8+ T cell responses were also observed in a hematological cancer model as well as a mesothelioma model (Jackaman et al., 2019; Lustgarten et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jackaman et al., 2019 and Lustgarten et al., 2004

claim: One study found that the growth of several tumor types was slower in aged mice, and this difference in growth rate was CD8+ T cell-dependent.
source: Paradoxically, one study found that the growth of several tumor types was slower in aged mice, and this difference in growth rate was CD8+ T cell-dependent (Oh et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oh et al., 2018

claim: Diet-induced obesity accelerates the age-associated decline of thymic function, resulting in reduced output of naïve T cells and TCR diversity.
source: For example, diet-induced obesity accelerates the age-associated decline of thymic function, resulting in reduced output of naïve T cells and TCR diversity (Yang et al., 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2009b

claim: Diet-induced obesity induces the accumulation of adipocytes in the bone marrow, which impairs hematopoiesis.
source: Just like aging, diet-induced obesity induces the accumulation of adipocytes in the bone marrow (Ambrosi et al., 2017), which impairs hematopoiesis (Naveiras et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ambrosi et al., 2017 and Naveiras et al., 2009

claim: Lymphatic transport, dendritic cell migration, and lymph node structure are reduced with obesity.
source: Secondary lymphoid organ function is also affected by obesity: lymphatic transport, dendritic cell migration, and lymph node structure are reduced (Weitman et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weitman et al., 2013

claim: Murine dendritic cells stimulate T cell responses less effectively in obesity.
source: and murine dendritic cells stimulate T cell responses less effectively in obesity (James et al., 2012; Mauro et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to James et al., 2012 and Mauro et al., 2017

claim: The prevalence of dysfunctional T cell populations is increased in obesity.
source: In addition, the prevalence of dysfunctional T cell populations is increased in obesity (Shirakawa et al., 2016; Spielmann et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Shirakawa et al., 2016, Spielmann et al., 2014, and Wang et al., 2019

claim: Higher frequencies of T cells expressing markers of antigen experience are present in the circulation of obese humans and animals.
source: and higher frequencies of T cells expressing markers of antigen experience are present in the circulation of obese humans and animals (Mauro et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019), similar to aged individuals.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mauro et al., 2017 and Wang et al., 2019

claim: Effective antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responses can be generated in obesity in certain contexts, such as infection of mice with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus.
source: Despite these challenges, effective antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responses can be generated in obesity in certain contexts, such as infection of mice with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) (Khan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khan et al., 2014

claim: The growth of syngeneic subcutaneous B16 melanoma, 4T1 breast, and 3LL lung carcinoma tumors is accelerated in C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet for 4–5 months.
source: The growth of syngeneic subcutaneous B16 melanoma, 4T1 breast, and 3LL lung carcinoma tumors is accelerated in C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 4–5 months (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019

claim: Accelerated tumor growth with obesity is associated with a dysfunctional CD8+ T cell phenotype, characterized by enhanced expression of co-inhibitory receptors and reduced expression of cytokines and the proliferation marker Ki-67.
source: This is associated with a dysfunctional CD8+ T cell phenotype, characterized by enhanced expression of co-inhibitory receptors and reduced expression of cytokines and the proliferation marker Ki-67.
evidence: Described as findings from Wang et al., 2019 study

claim: The CD8+ T cell defect with obesity is CD8+ T cell-intrinsic, as it is also present with ex vivo T cell activation.
source: This defect is CD8+ T cell-intrinsic, as it is also present with ex vivo T cell activation.
evidence: Described as findings from Wang et al., 2019 study

claim: A reduced anti-tumor CD8+ T cell response was found with diet-induced obesity in a murine breast cancer model.
source: Another study also found a reduced anti-tumor CD8+ T cell response with diet-induced obesity in a murine breast cancer model (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020

claim: Reduced T cell infiltration was described in obese colorectal cancer patients.
source: For example, reduced T cell infiltration was described in obese colorectal cancer patients
evidence: Described as evidence from Wang et al., 2019 study

claim: Increased expression of markers of T cell exhaustion, including co-inhibitory receptor PD-1, was seen in tumor-infiltrating T cells in obese melanoma patients.
source: and increased expression of markers of T cell exhaustion, including co-inhibitory receptor PD-1, was seen in tumor-infiltrating T cells in obese melanoma patients (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019

claim: Age-induced thymic involution can be decreased by long-term dietary restriction, thereby enhancing thymic output in aged mice.
source: First, age-induced thymic involution can be decreased by long-term dietary restriction, thereby enhancing thymic output in aged mice (Yang et al., 2009a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2009a

claim: Feeding of a calorically restricted diet for 13 to 18 years leads to preservation of T cell functions with age in non-human primates, in addition to increased naïve T cell numbers and TCR repertoire.
source: Second, feeding of a calorically restricted diet for 13 to 18 years leads to preservation of T cell functions with age in non-human primates, in addition to increased naïve T cell numbers and TCR repertoire (Messaoudi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Messaoudi et al., 2006

claim: Dietary restriction induces a reduction of memory T cells in secondary lymphoid organs and circulation but an accumulation in the bone marrow, resulting in increased protection from both infectious and tumor challenges.
source: Finally, dietary restriction induces a reduction of memory T cells in secondary lymphoid organs and circulation but an accumulation in the bone marrow, resulting in increased protection from both infectious and tumor challenges (Collins et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins et al., 2019

claim: A short-term (48 hr) fast enhances the efficacy of chemotherapy in the murine fibrosarcoma model MCA205 in a T cell-dependent manner.
source: For example, a short-term (48 hr) fast enhances the efficacy of chemotherapy in the murine fibrosarcoma model MCA205 in a T cell-dependent manner (Pietrocola et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pietrocola et al., 2016

claim: Caloric restriction mimetics, including ATP citrate lyase inhibitor hydroxycitrate, reduce tumor growth in chemotherapy-treated mice similarly to short-term fasting, in a manner dependent on CD8+ T cells.
source: CRMs, including ATP citrate lyase inhibitor hydroxycitrate, reduce tumor growth in chemotherapy-treated mice similarly to short-term fasting, in a manner dependent on CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Described as findings from Pietrocola et al., 2016 study

claim: A low calorie fasting-mimicking diet in combination with chemotherapy shows benefit in the 4T1 breast cancer and B16 melanoma models.
source: Another study demonstrated similar findings with the 4T1 breast cancer and B16 melanoma models, using a low calorie FMD in combination with chemotherapy (Di Biase et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Biase et al., 2016

claim: The numbers of common lymphoid progenitors in the bone marrow as well as circulating CD8+ T cells are increased by fasting-mimicking diet.
source: Systemically, the numbers of common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) in the bone marrow as well as circulating CD8+ T cells are increased by FMD (Di Biase et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Biase et al., 2016

claim: A low-protein diet reduced tumor progression in murine lymphoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma and melanoma models in a CD8+ T cell-dependent manner.
source: Rubio-Patiño et al. found that a low-protein diet reduced tumor progression in murine lymphoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma and melanoma models in a CD8+ T cell-dependent manner (Rubio-Patiño et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rubio-Patiño et al., 2018

claim: Dietary methionine restriction can have anti-cancer effects.
source: For example, dietary methionine restriction, which promotes lifespan and metabolic health in mice (Ables et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2005), can have anti-cancer effects (Gao et al., 2019; Wanders et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: A shift in macrophage polarization accompanied by increased intratumoral CD8+ T cell numbers and GzmB expression occurs in mice fed a methionine-restricted diet.
source: Accordingly, a shift in macrophage polarization accompanied by increased intratumoral CD8+ T cell numbers and GzmB expression occurs in mice fed a methionine-restricted diet (Orillion et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Orillion et al., 2018

claim: When naïve T cells are activated by ligation of the TCR and costimulatory signals, they initiate a phase of rapid growth, differentiation, and proliferation accompanied by a switch from a quiescent metabolic state to a highly metabolically active state.
source: When naïve T cells are activated by ligation of the TCR and costimulatory signals, they initiate a phase of rapid growth, differentiation, and proliferation (Smith-Garvin et al., 2009). This transition is accompanied by a switch from a quiescent metabolic state, characterized by mostly oxidative metabolism, to a highly metabolically active state, characterized by the use of anabolic pathways such as anaerobic glycolysis, glutaminolysis, and one-carbon metabolism (Chang et al., 2013; Ho et al., 2015; Ron-Harel et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Glycolysis directly impacts translation of IFN-γ mRNA in activated T cells.
source: For example, glycolysis directly impacts translation of IFN-γ mRNA (Chang et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2013

claim: Memory T cells and Tregs rely on oxidative metabolic pathways, including fatty acid oxidation.
source: In contrast to effector T cells, memory T cells and Tregs rely on oxidative metabolic pathways, including fatty acid oxidation (FAO) (Michalek et al., 2011; Pearce et al., 2009; van der Windt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Manipulating metabolism is sufficient to change the differentiation of T cells toward distinct phenotypes in many cases.
source: In many cases, manipulating metabolism is sufficient to change the differentiation of T cells toward distinct phenotypes, indicating that certain metabolic pathways lie upstream of fate decisions in T cells (Buck et al., 2016; Michalek et al., 2011; Pearce et al., 2009; Pollizzi et al., 2016; Verbist et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The anabolic metabolic program characteristic of effector T cells is orchestrated by mammalian target of rapamycin, Myc, and hypoxia-inducible factor-1α.
source: The anabolic metabolic program characteristic of effector T cells is orchestrated by mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), Myc, and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)−1α, which are engaged during T cell activation (Pollizzi and Powell, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pollizzi and Powell, 2014

claim: Memory T cell metabolism is promoted by AMP-activated protein kinase, which is activated during low energy conditions and opposes signaling through mTOR.
source: In contrast, memory T cell metabolism is promoted by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) – a nutrient sensor that is activated during low energy conditions and opposes signaling through mTOR, which is activated by high nutrient levels (Pollizzi and Powell, 2014; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pollizzi and Powell, 2014 and Figure 3

claim: Memory T cell generation is promoted by metformin-induced AMPK activation as well as rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition.
source: Accordingly, memory T cell generation is promoted by metformin-induced AMPK activation as well as rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition (Araki et al., 2009; Pearce et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Araki et al., 2009 and Pearce et al., 2009

claim: Various interventions that promote oxidative, mitochondrial metabolic pathways in T cells enhance their anti-tumor function.
source: Various interventions that promote oxidative, mitochondrial metabolic pathways in T cells enhance their anti-tumor function, for example promoting mitochondrial fusion, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, supplementing arginine, inducing fatty acid metabolism, and inhibiting glutamine metabolism (Buck et al., 2016; Chowdhury et al., 2018; Geiger et al., 2016; Leone et al., 2019; Scharping et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Rapamycin can promote anti-tumor immunity in certain contexts, such as the MOC1 oral cancer model.
source: However, rapamycin can also promote anti-tumor immunity in certain contexts, such as the MOC1 oral cancer model (Cash et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cash et al., 2015 and Moore et al., 2016

claim: T cell-intrinsic AMPK signaling is required for T cell responses, including anti-tumor immunity, by promoting metabolic fitness and survival.
source: On the other hand, T cell-intrinsic AMPK signaling is also required for T cell responses, including anti-tumor immunity, by promoting metabolic fitness and survival (Blagih et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Blagih et al., 2015 and Rao et al., 2015

claim: The AMPK activator metformin promotes anti-tumor T cell responses through several mechanisms, including AMPK activation in T cells.
source: Indeed, the AMPK activator metformin promotes anti-tumor T cell responses through several mechanisms, including AMPK activation in T cells (Eikawa et al., 2015), AMPK-dependent degradation of inhibitory ligand PD-L1 (Cha et al., 2018), and reduced oxygen consumption in tumor cells, likely resulting from AMPK-independent inhibition of the electron transport chain by metformin (Scharping et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Aging is a process characterized by widespread metabolic and signaling changes including mitochondrial dysfunction and dysregulation of nutrient sensing.
source: Aging is a process characterized by widespread metabolic and signaling changes impacting many of the pathways highlighted above (Barzilai et al., 2012), which may affect anti-tumor T cell responses. Specific metabolic changes considered hallmarks of aging are mitochondrial dysfunction and dysregulation of nutrient sensing (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barzilai et al., 2012 and López-Otín et al., 2013

claim: Inhibition of insulin, insulin-like growth factor-1, or mTOR signaling increases lifespan, and so does enhancing AMPK signaling.
source: Underscoring the importance of metabolism in regulating lifespan and aging, inhibition of insulin, insulin-like growth factor (IGF)−1, or mTOR signaling increases lifespan, and so does enhancing AMPK signaling (López-Otín et al., 2016; López-Otín et al., 2013; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by citations to López-Otín et al., 2016 and 2013, and Figure 3

claim: Inhibition of mTOR signaling improves hematopoiesis in aged mice as well as immune function in the contexts of vaccination and infection in elderly humans.
source: mTOR signaling also impacts immunity in aging: inhibition of mTOR signaling improves hematopoiesis in aged mice as well as immune function in the contexts of vaccination and infection in elderly humans (Chen et al., 2009; Mannick et al., 2018; Mannick et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Inhibition of pro-inflammatory NF-κB signaling can reduce aging phenotypes.
source: Systemic inflammation is similarly associated with aging – often referred to as 'inflammaging' (López-Otín et al., 2013), and this contributes to aging-related decline, as evidenced for example by the observation that inhibition of pro-inflammatory NF-κB signaling can reduce aging phenotypes (Tilstra et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tilstra et al., 2012

claim: T cells may contribute to age-related inflammation and its metabolic complications, such as hyperglycemia.
source: Interestingly, recent research demonstrated that T cells may contribute to age-related inflammation and its metabolic complications, such as hyperglycemia (Bharath et al., 2020; Desdín-Micó et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Aged T cells are characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: For example, aged T cells are characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction (Ron-Harel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ron-Harel et al., 2018

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction in aged T cells results in defective respiratory capacity and one-carbon metabolism, and supplementation with one-carbon metabolites can improve aged T cell activation and survival.
source: This results in defective respiratory capacity and one-carbon metabolism, and supplementation with one-carbon metabolites, like formate and glycine, can improve aged T cell activation and survival (Ron-Harel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ron-Harel et al., 2018

claim: Both mitochondrial dysfunction and autophagy contribute to inflammatory phenotypes in aged T cells, and this can be improved by the AMPK activator metformin.
source: Both mitochondrial dysfunction and autophagy contribute to inflammatory phenotypes in aged T cells, and this can be improved by the AMPK activator metformin (Bharath et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bharath et al., 2020

claim: Mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, through complex formation with sestrins, directly contributes to aged T cell dysfunction.
source: Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling, through complex formation with a class of stress response proteins known as sestrins, directly contribute to aged T cell dysfunction (Lanna et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lanna et al., 2017

claim: Aged CD8+ Tvm cells have enhanced respiratory capacity despite being dysfunctional.
source: For example, aged CD8+ Tvm cell were recently shown to have enhanced respiratory capacity despite being dysfunctional (Quinn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quinn et al., 2020

claim: Aged memory CD8+ T cells may have increased mTOR activity and glycolysis as well as a reduced ability to engage in autophagy.
source: Furthermore, aged memory CD8+ T cells may have increased mTOR activity and glycolysis well as a reduced ability to engage in autophagy (Davenport et al., 2019; Henson et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Davenport et al., 2019 and Henson et al., 2014

claim: Newly activated aged CD4+ T cells fail to induce glycolysis as robustly as younger counterparts.
source: while newly activated aged CD4+ T cells fail to induce glycolysis as robustly as younger counterparts (Ron-Harel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ron-Harel et al., 2018

claim: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are characterized by insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and inflammation, collectively leading to the metabolic syndrome.
source: Like aging, obesity is characterized by profound systemic changes in both humans and animal models, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and inflammation, collectively leading to the so-called metabolic syndrome (Barzilai et al., 2012; Huang, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barzilai et al., 2012 and Huang, 2009

claim: Adipose tissue inflammation plays a key role in the pathophysiology of metabolic syndrome.
source: Adipose tissue inflammation plays a key role in the pathophysiology of metabolic syndrome, and adipose tissue secretion of adipokines, such as the satiety regulator leptin, and inflammatory cytokines into the circulation contributes to systemic inflammatory and metabolic dysregulation (Bremer and Jialal, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bremer and Jialal, 2013

claim: Infiltration of CD8+ and inflammatory CD4+ T cells into adipose tissue is increased with obesity, while CD4+ Tregs are reduced, contributing to adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance.
source: Specifically, infiltration of CD8+ and inflammatory CD4+ T cells into adipose tissue is increased with obesity, while CD4+ Tregs are reduced, contributing to adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance (Feuerer et al., 2009; Nishimura et al., 2009; Winer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are characterized by mTOR activation.
source: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are characterized by mTOR activation (Liu and Sabatini, 2020; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Sabatini, 2020 and Figure 3

claim: mTOR hyperactivation contributes to development of the metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance, as well as chronic inflammation.
source: mTOR hyperactivation contributes to development of the metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance, as well as chronic inflammation, for example by promoting inflammatory cytokine secretion by cells of the innate immune system in the liver and adipose tissue (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu and Sabatini, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2014 and Liu and Sabatini, 2020

claim: Chronic inflammation associated with obesity is thought to promote the dysfunctional T cell states.
source: In turn, chronic inflammation associated with obesity is thought to promote the dysfunctional T cell states described above (Shirakawa et al., 2016; Spielmann et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In the context of influenza infection with HFD feeding, C57BL/6 mouse CD8+ T cells display a shift toward oxidative metabolism accompanied by defective memory T cell responses.
